title: What would have been a better way to handle the sexual scenes in Saltburn?

commenti.body:
I don’t think he needed to have sex with the grave.  The fact he was hugging and kissing it was more than enough to show how desperate, pathetic, and obsessed he was.  They could have cut there, or at the very most waited for him to unbuckle his pants or take his shirt off.  It’s pretty obvious where the whole scene is going from the second he unbuttons his shirt, and the extended scene that follows is basically unnecessary and just there for the sake of being shocking/edgy.

In addition, they could have just shown him stick his head up the sister’s skirt and than cut to that shot of him sitting in the bathtub with blood on his lips.  We know what happened, we know how weird it is.  It tells us everything we need to know without feeling like it was just there for the sake of being “dark” and “uncomfortable”.

To be honest though, none of this would really fix the film.  I don’t have any issue with it being over the top, I just think it’s a pretty shallow film all around.  It’s a fun, well shot movie, but not a particularly good one at the end of the day.

Interesting points! I definitely can agree that it was still a fun experience for me once I accepted that my initial idea wasn’t what the film was going for, but still not really a monumental film or anything. 

Definitely like your points about the scenes being shorter. I hadn’t thought about it that way, but I can see how the grave scene might have been stronger if it was cut after he unbuckled his pants. Makes me wonder how much of it could have been better if it wasn’t so intent on drawing out the absurd details.

The sex scenes weren't the problem, the hollowness was. Changing the sex scenes doesn't change anything really besides how uncomfortable certain audience members feel for 30 seconds in some scenes. The main character just didn't feel consistent at all, either in how his actions related to his feelings, or his motivations.

Yeah, good points about Oliver. He definitely was lackluster and bit more flat than I was expecting. I guess what I meant to ask is what you would have wanted to see in terms of his character or other characters in relation to the scenes. How could they have been better connected to the character to make it feel less disjointed and non-substantial? For me, a bit more depth in Oliver’s obsession rather than shifting the focus away from it might have been nice. Or just anything to make Oliver feel a bit more dimensional in his obsessions and tendency to rely on sexuality to become close to other characters. 

Sorry if that’s still not really making much sense. English isn’t my first language and I’m struggling to figure out exactly how to word myself here. Thanks for the response though!

I liked the movie. Unabashedly. At a younger age, probably would have loved it. 

I've gone pretty far down the disturbing movie iceberg, so my standards for shock are a bit different. Labeling it shock porn is like using torture porn to describe every horror movie with hyper-violence. It's a bit lazy, but I get that you're using it as short hand to get to your argument. Fair enough.

The sex scenes take place in a world that's numb and degenerate. The family has no idea how to process emotion in a healthy way, and the sex scenes, which are idealized by SOCIETY as intimate acts, explore how ruined these people are. I don't think they were out of place or "just for shock value" at all.

It’s not hollow. One of the most frustrating things this year has been the misunderstanding of Saltburn. I don’t think it’s the best movie ever or beyond criticism. But it’s gotten a raw deal when it comes to people recognizing what’s going on.

The movie is about changes in who has power. The Cattons represent the traditional archetype. While Oliver is the next wave. Think about modern politics and the amount of grifters who have worked their way into positions of power. Or social media and the grifters who have worked their way into insane followings.

The more specific discussion is about style versus substance. And how the world appreciates style more than it does substance.

That’s the thesis. That how you present yourself matters more than who you really are and what you’re doing. 

So it’s about a certain kind of person in a specific era. Which puts it in the same category as American Psycho, The Social Network, and Ingrid  Goes West.

But you have a majority of people online, especially critics, either saying the movie is empty or is a bad version of Parasite. When it’s neither of those things. Again, just because it has themes doesn’t mean it’s a masterpiece or beyond criticism. I’m just saying the current popular criticisms aren’t accurate. 

It’s kind of like when Fight Club came out, you had people saying it was just a fighting movie. You can criticize Fight Club for a lot but it’s not just a fighting movie.

[Full Saltburn breakdown](https://filmcolossus.com/saltburn-2023-explained)

Thanks for the response! English isn’t my first language so finding the right description for what I wanted to say was pretty hard. I didn’t mean to sound lazy with my description, I’m was just trying to find the best way to phrase it.

I did enjoy the movie a bit too, but it definitely clashed with my expectations — which is definitely my fault. I think when it was framed at the beginning with Oliver’s speech “I loved him…” made it seem like the frame of perspective would be on him and Felix, rather than the family as a whole which made it difficult at times to get the point of some of it if that makes sense? 

I definitely think maybe I need to give it another watch with a different perspective though. So thank you for your thoughts!

Thank you for explaining! I think the way you described it makes the overall picture make more sense. I’ve never seen Parasite so I don’t really understand the comparisons people make with it, but I definitely think I got the wrong idea of the thesis and where the frame stood. 

I did enjoy the movie but I think I may have just had the wrong idea from my interpretation of Oliver’s introduction lines, which is ultimately my fault.

It’s okay! It’s happening a lot lol.

It doesn’t help that the people who are supposed to help others see this stuff, film critics, are the ones spreading the wrong idea of the movie.

Exactly.  9 times out of 10, the mind will come up with something much scarier or more messed up than anything they could get in a film.  Leaving things up to the audience’s imagination is sometimes wayyyy more uncomfortable than just showing us.  The same goes for the ending of Saltburn.  I already knew he was responsible for everything a good while before they showed the “how he did it” montage.  My imagination made the events so much more interesting than what we were finally shown.  Even if they had only shown him puncture the bike tire, it would have sent the viewer’s mind into overdrive thinking of how he did what he did.

This is why I love movies like Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Cure.  It didn’t give a single easy answer, and trying to rationalize or understand the events after the movie was over scared me so much more than when I was actively watching the film.

The sex scenes were meant to showcase both Oliver's obsession with Felix & the lengths he would go to use his power to dominate other members of the family. There's a stark juxtaposition there, I know, but that's because Oliver was overcome with lust for Felix's prowess & simply saw sex with >!Venetia!< as a way in the family circle.
I agree, I think if watched it again I'd come away with a different mood. The movie also mentioned one of my favorite authors ever Evelyn Waugh, which was like a cool easter egg for me.
